en: Furthermore, I have occasionally perused the scriptures of the Śākya school.

Although the establishment of its teachings primarily emphasizes emptiness and stillness, its admonitions against deception and delusion, and its methods for eliminating anger and restraining desire, are essentially no different from the Way of encouraging good and punishing evil.
Since the rise of the School of the Gate (Chán), five lineages have successively branched out from Caoxi, each with its own writings. During the Song dynasty...
After the Jingde era, [the records] were compiled into the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp) and subsequent works.
Subsequently, another person extracted the essential points and synthesized them into a single volume titled the *Wu Deng Hui Yuan* (The Five Lamps Metaphorically Combined).

Later, during our own dynasty, the śramaṇa Hai-kuan, mindful that the lineages had proliferated extensively yet lacked a comprehensive account spanning several hundred years from the Song, Jin, Yuan, and Ming dynasties, thereupon composed this work.

This work is a continuation of the previous record. Now, the monk Chaoyong of Shenggan Temple, fearing that the genealogical registers would gradually become disordered and that oral reports and observations would remain inconsistent, conducted extensive research and broad investigations.
He took the two preceding compilations as his standard for adjudication and collated them;
he excised redundancies and superfluities while augmenting what was incomplete, thereby completing the entire work. His dedication to this task may truly be called diligent. Up to...
Regarding the words recorded in these documents that corroborate one another, there are many rare analogies and indirect metaphors used in their exposition;

yet their essential purport and ultimate aim are solely to dispel delusion and restore the true nature of reality, not exceeding the intent of "restraining the heterodox to preserve sincerity" and "instructing others toward goodness.
This is not merely beneficial for the doctrinal principles of the Chan school.
This is all. Therefore, I have composed this preface.
On the twenty-fifth day of the fourth month in the thirty-second year of the Kangxi era.
Preface to the Table of Contents for the Complete Record of the Five Lamps.
I reverently consider that since the founding of this Great Dynasty, the governance of the state has surpassed that of the Three Dynasties.
Regarding all matters pertaining to moral transformation and instruction, they have been fully promoted and disseminated. [This applies to] the History of the Sangha...
The *Chuan deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), though an essential scripture for those beyond the secular world, ought likewise to be periodically revised and clarified.
(Yong) therefore reflected that the lineage of wisdom from the past was at stake; thus, casting aside my own rustic ignorance, I entered the capital in the *guihai* year of the Kangxi era.
I extensively sought out and widely gathered materials, carefully investigating the events recorded in the various collections of the past and present.
As for those passages that are factually true but whose reasoning is inappropriate or which contain redundant and spurious elements, they shall be deleted.

As for those whose essential meaning is non-dual and whose mechanisms are in profound accord with reality, they shall be augmented. Thereafter, the lineages shall be examined and verified, and the great principles shall be clarified, so as not to allow gold and brass to be mixed together;
the intent is to ensure that all branches and details are fully elucidated, such that every citation, explanation, and analysis possesses its own root.
He exhaustively searched and investigated every source, compiling a work of over two million words entitled the *Wudeng Quanshu* (Complete Book of the Five Lamps).
He encountered a sagely Son of Heaven—
a ruler who governs with the compassion and virtue of the Ultimate Way— whereby all things in heaven and earth enjoy clarity, tranquility, peace, and abundance.
Buddhism has been able to assist in the great transformation [of the realm].
Among the emperors of antiquity, none has enlightened the common people as Your Majesty has; none has been so earnest in desiring that they turn their hearts toward the Way.
(Eternal) Therefore, with diligent and sincere devotion, and without avoiding the risk of offense, I have ventured to present this treatise for Your Majesty’s consideration. May it be well received.
In the leisure moments between the myriad affairs of state,
[the Emperor] was able to peruse this scripture and correct its errors and discrepancies;
he then graciously bestowed upon it a preface.
The celestial chapters shine like clouds, and the sagely compositions surge like waves.
Externally, they verify the Six Classics; internally, they encompass the Three Pitakas. Thus, the thousand lamps reflect one another, becoming even more manifest through the Emperor’s composition;
the myriad species find common refuge, for which we are deeply grateful.

The imperial decree has become all the more penetrating; it does not merely extol the good and suppress the evil, but clearly distinguishes between Confucianism and Chan, forging a mold for the four quarters of heaven and establishing a model for a hundred generations.
Furthermore, I have been graced with the distribution of the *Lifan* (Inner Treasury) edition.
Having received the imperial decree,
we have exerted our efforts to assemble the craftsmen.
We now present the newly carved Imperial Preface along with the first volume of the complete work.
The Imperial Majesty was greatly pleased.
He issued a handwritten edict to [Ling]yong, saying: "After the imperial preface, it would be well to include a preface by yourself regarding the general principles and conventions.
[Ling]yong felt abashed beyond measure and dared not fail to prostrate himself and offer these words: "Our Buddha, with the Eye of the True Dharma, established this One Great Teaching."
Its school takes the non-transmission of the intent as the progenitor of the Great Teaching.

This school is the source of the Way of the mind-nature and the wondrous truth of all living beings. Its progenitor is the great model of concentration and wisdom, the true verification of luminous awakening.
Now, His Majesty the Great Sage has graciously perused this compilation and promoted the principle of the unity of Confucianism and Buddhism for its widespread circulation.
As it is said,
the way in which a sage establishes his teachings must...

Only the sages were able to practice it. Is this not not only the great good fortune of the followers of the Buddha for ten thousand generations, but also the great good fortune of all the people of the world?
Thus, Jing composed this preface.
Written on the eighth day of the first intercalary month of the *guīyǒu* year of the *Kāngxī* era by the monk (Subject Chao Yong),
Successor of the Patriarchs at Shenggan Temple.
Preface to the *Wǔdēng quánshū*.

The dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds have many divergent sources. What is valued is grasping the collar and lifting the main framework, while skillfully effecting reduction or augmentation.
As for the essentials of such grasping and lifting, one should rely on the original teachings (*mūladharma*) rather than seeking proof in derivative streams;
one should rely on the Buddha’s own words rather than seeking proof in worldly discourse. Thus, one attains the Great Mean of the world.
The principle of rectitude begins to leap forth. Knowing how to dispel ignorance and shake off the fallen leaves, one traverses all paths without contradiction;
with universal illumination free from partiality, one reveals the true essence throughout the past and present. This is what is called the "Great Matter" (mahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya).
It is for this Great Matter that the Tathāgata appeared in the world, taking the essentials of the True Dharma as that Great Matter.
The essence of this teaching was transmitted through secret succession, serving as the progenitor of a single great school.

As it has been passed down from generation to generation, the five lamps have maintained their connection like a continuous supply of firewood; this indeed has its origins. Reading these texts and examining these events, some manifest perfect faculties, like ripples weaving across a pond;
others roar with lion-like cries, like thunder crashing through a deep ravine. Those whose hearts are intoxicated by them find such excellence sweeter than *amṛta*.

The *Amṛta* (Ghee). Those who have mistakenly touched it find its potency more fierce than poison. Because the texts transmitted by hand have varied from one another, they have become obscure and blurred, leading people to harbor doubts and lack faith.
Thus, errors and corruptions have emerged in abundance, such that the distinction between fish eyes and pearls, or between common shells and precious gems, can no longer be made.
Is this due to some deficiency on the part of those who received and transmitted the teachings? Or is it rather the fault of those who recorded them? Since the time of the Sage has passed...

The lineages of the masters have each adopted their own partial views. Were it not for those possessing eyes that transcend the mundane, who employ a heart of great public impartiality and selflessness to unify all schools;

who extensively propagate the succession and establish the guiding principles, and who diligently sift through the teachings to strictly determine what to accept and reject—how could the sun and stars not grow dim, and the vast ocean not run dry? As for Kāśyapa’s [teachings] within the scriptures and doctrines...
Externally, he transmitted the *Akṣaya-samādhi* to Mahākauravya. After twenty-eight transmissions, it reached the Venerable Bodhidharma.
According to the *Book of Tang*, at the end of the Northern Wei dynasty, there was a monk named Bodhidharma. He was originally the son of the King of India;
having renounced the world to protect his kingdom, he entered the Southern Sea and attained the sublime Dharma of the Chan school. From himself—
Śākyamuni Buddha transmitted his robe and bowl as a token of succession through the generations. He entered the Liang dynasty and remained hidden at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song.
He transmitted his Dharma to Huike; Huike to Sengcan; Sengcan to Daoxin;
Daoxin to Hongren; and Hongren to Huineng. Huineng resided in China and was thus the sixth generation from Bodhidharma. Therefore...
The world calls him the Sixth Patriarch; his writings may indeed be examined in detail.
Furthermore, he reflected that the Eye of the True Dharma and the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa can be expressed through language, yet cannot be reached by language alone.

Therefore, at the conclusion, he specifically and solemnly performed the act of picking up a flower as an entrustment, thereby demonstrating that the True Dharma is not something characterized by flattery or crookedness.
The words of Mingjiao Yongshou Song state: "The True Dharma is that from which the Great Teaching originates;
it is that by which all the scriptures are elucidated. One who attains this, though they may speak in ten thousand ways, what they say has never been confused.
One who does not attain this, though they maintain it through the cessation of speech, what they maintain has never [been unified]."
From the beginning, he was free from delusion. His skillful exposition of the essential Dharma was such that nothing surpassed his enlightened teaching.
In the present age, the path of the Dharma has declined; false teachers have appeared, wallowing in power and profit, and throwing their arms about in strife.
These wretched and deceitful fellows treat the Buddha as a mere plaything, while regarding the path of language and scripture as a mere byway.
In the past, these were employed to extol and uphold the essential tenets; now, they are used to gnaw and erode the lion’s own body.

Those who bear the responsibility for the life-force of wisdom have no leisure even to gaze at the rafters and wring their hands in frustration; what further need is there to labor over exposition or critical appraisal?
This was done to commemorate the ritual traditions of our predecessors. My elder brother, Shenxue Ji, felt profound grief and indignation at this;
he therefore exhausted his deliberations and thoughts, laboring over brush and inkstone, and applied himself with thirty years of painstaking effort.
The entire work has now been completed from its draft, having received the repeated commendation of His Majesty the Emperor.
The date for carving the printing blocks is approaching; thus, the ancestral Way shines once more and the Five Lamps blaze forth again.
I, [Name], though of dull wit and obscure understanding, have also been permitted to take up my clumsy brush to assist in this meritorious achievement.
Furthermore, they whispered among themselves, leaping for joy and praising him, seeking to affiliate themselves with the You and Xia of the Confucian school.
Now, the Way is the foundation of the world; the scriptures are the traces of the world; and affairs are the diversities of the world.

Principle is the commonality of the world; by means of its traces, the source is revealed. By resolving this commonality, differences are harmonized, such that from antiquity to the present, there is no redundant meaning.
Is this not the clear verification for grasping the fundamental principles and providing evidence through supplementation or subtraction?
Ziyang’s discourse on Bodhidharma was able to completely overturn conventional molds and inaugurate the Chan school.

The study of the *Yìxué* (Meaning of the Teachings) is particularly sublime; one thus knows that the essence of the Separate Transmission has long endured within the world, serving to inspire the profound faith of both the monastic and lay communities.
All discussion relies entirely upon paper and ink as its evidentiary basis.
At the end of the Song dynasty, the Five Lamps were transmitted together, and Master Dàchuān Jìgōng compiled and carved them into woodblocks. To this day, more than five hundred years have passed.
Those who have inherited the Dharma number in the thousands. Though these lineages have been intermittent and fragmented, my elder brother Jì has brought them forth in this record.

His intent in reviving what was extinguished and continuing what was severed is as vast as the Great Void; how could he be like the faction of Băiyán, who suppresses others to exalt their own kind and treats the rise and fall of lineages as a matter for editorial revision?

He merely recounts what has been transmitted without claiming original authorship, humbly comparing himself to Lǎopéng. May those who understand me forgive me, and may those who condemn me likewise do so.
Although I am Confucius, there is that which I cannot avoid. My elder brother Ji first built a thatched hut on Yunwai Peak in Yongjia;

for eight years, through both cold and heat, he tilled with the blade and cultivated by fire, severing all ties to worldly affairs. He began the project of transcribing the complete scriptures at the foot of the peak.
When Master Dao sent him a letter, it expressed a very deep concern that he might not be able to bring the work to completion. However—
Now that this book is completed, it may be presented to the Elder in the Land of Quiescent Light. (Kui) In the past, I was deeply favored by the Elder’s profound affection;
therefore, I have appended this to the end of the preface to demonstrate the difficulty of bringing a literary work to completion.
Furthermore, my elder brother Ji has upheld the Master’s teachings, assisted in the propagation of the Dharma, and supported the scriptures; what he preserves is vast.

What is perceived here is vast. Although the origins of their training and inclinations may differ from those of the Confucians, once the Five Lamps were established, they proceeded in parallel with the *Book of Changes*, the *Book of Rites*, the *Book of Poetry*, the *Book of Documents*, and the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, acting as their counterparts. It is just like this.
Composed by the śramaṇa Chao Kui of the Ancient Huayan Temple at Jingming Garden on Mount Yuquan in Beijing,
during the winter of the Renshen year of the Kangxi era.
Memorial for the Presentation of the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps.
I, the monk (Chao Yong), Abbot of Shenggan Temple, respectfully submit this memorial regarding the presentation of the *Wudeng Quanshu* (Complete Book of the Five Lamps).
I humbly consider that the three teachings share one and the same Way, and that the sages possess no dual hearts.
Although their traces differ—between those of the secular world and those beyond it—their underlying principle is fundamentally the same: the cultivation of oneself for the benefit of others.
As for these distinctions: when categories are intermingled, the words of various schools are esteemed;
yet to achieve a balanced synthesis, the lineages must be clarified, so that their origins may serve as a reliable foundation.

Fortunate to have encountered this era of universal civilization, I respectfully compile the perfected teachings of this single school. I do not presume to say that my contribution is as significant as dust or dew.
Regarding the lofty heights and profound depths of mountains and seas,
I truly rely upon Your Majesty’s sagely brilliance to illuminate the sunlit path through the darkness of the world. This is because I humbly encounter Your Majesty,
the Emperor, below.
The mind-transmission of a thousand sages and the Way that surpasses a hundred kings—
his vision was clear and his hearing acute, such that even the words of those nearby were scrutinized.
Bells are suspended and gongs are set; when good news is heard, they are raised aloft. The myriad regions look up together to the Sage who possesses the Way;
the four seas have long sung the praises of the Son of Heaven in Great Peace.
I, the subject Seng Chao-yong, am an unworthy member of the monastic community, yet I have had the good fortune to rely upon [the Emperor].
In the Purple Forbidden City, I harbor deep devotion yet find no way to repay it; my vow is unwavering and directed toward nothing else.

Thus I reflect upon the Buddha’s arising in Western India and the Patriarchs’ transmission to Eastern China: they take the realization of mind and the seeing of nature as their core principle, and the transformation of evil into goodness as their teaching.
In practice, they take the six perfections as the Great Vehicle, fundamentally not departing from the mundane world.
One seeks the true mark by examining appearances; in attaining realization, taking up insight through contemplation is the essential principle.
There is nothing here that does not borrow expedient words to manifest the ultimate truth. As for those who recorded its lineage, they still exist from former generations.
Those among us today who would take up its branch must now urgently examine it in detail. I, the monk [Your Subject], disregarding my own meager learning, have devoted myself to this for ten years.
I have examined the surviving records from antiquity and searched through the lineages of recent times. Their words do not diverge, and their teachings accord with the lamp of the mind.
In the Western Regions, the lineage begins with the Seven Buddhas and is transmitted successively to Kāśyapa and Ānanda;
in the Central Land, it begins with Bodhidharma and flows down through Qingyuan and Nanyue. As for the later branches, the details of their dharma heirs remain uncertain.

In the interim, he gathered the sages and worthies who appeared through transformation; nearly three thousand years have passed since that time, and there are over seven thousand individuals in total.
Sixteen volumes are designated as their titles, and one hundred and twenty volumes record their words.
Although this is known as the *Complete Book of the Five Lamps*, it is indeed still incomplete.
The Celestial Mind clearly observes all; for this reason, I have compiled these writings and venture to present them.
I humbly pray that you will not reject these words, however crude they may be.
I humbly entreat Your Majesty to graciously consider this.

If it is deemed worthy to be included as a successor to the tradition, and if you would permit it to be appended to the final volume of the *Lóngzàng* (Dragon Treasury), then the lineage will flourish for generations. I hope that a single, definitive edition may be collated and carved into woodblocks to be displayed for posterity.

[Your] Subject, the Monk, has further been graced by Your Majesty’s compassionate inspection of the sublime virtues of former sages, for which there are records in the Buddhist scriptures (*Nèidiǎn*). Previously...
I am honored to have my name at the head of this volume.
If Your Majesty would deign to grant a preface, it would constitute an epochal celebration for ten thousand years;
thus, the Wheel of Dharma shall rely upon the Golden Wheel to turn forevermore.
The sun of Shun reflects upon the sun of the Buddha, causing its brilliance to increase all the more.
(Your servant), the monk Chao Yong, cannot help but gaze toward Heaven and look up to the Sage with the utmost intensity and trepidation. I hereby respectfully submit this.
Submitted: Respectfully presented for the Imperial perusal.

The 3rd day of the 3rd month in the 32nd year of the Kangxi era. (Subject) Monk (Chao Yong), Abbot of Shenggan Temple, (Subject) Monk Chao Yong, respectfully submits this memorial for the presentation of the *Wudeng Quanshu* (Complete Book of the Five Lamps). (Part II).
Respectfully submitted by (Subject) Monk Chao Yong, Abbot of Shenggan Temple.
A Memorial on the Presentation of the Complete Collection of the Five Lamps (Wǔdēng Quánshū).
I humbly reflect that as transformation permeates the Great Harmony, the Way contains all within its vastness and breadth.

I pray that the virtues of the Supreme Vehicle may be bestowed, universally covering and impartially sustaining all beings. May the teaching of goodness be spread for the benefit of the people, and the heart of compassion be distributed throughout the world.
To nurture all creatures, we most reverently encounter this grand ceremony and joyfully find ourselves at this flourishing epoch. This is because we now humbly behold Your Majesty,
the Emperor, who possesses the reverence of Yao and the wisdom of Shun.
His literary achievements and martial prowess are ever renewed through his sagely learning; he pacifies the myriad states by establishing the ultimate standard, and his imperial majesty spreads afar.
He unifies the six provinces to secure the Way, suspending the celestial mirror within the realm and wielding great authority.
Within the realm, the deserts were cleared and pacified entirely by the direction of Your Majesty’s sagacious calculations;
the determination of heaven and earth was entirely due to the strategic maneuvers of Your divine ingenuity.
Looking back with favor upon those who provided protection, you purified the ancestral lineage within the Zen groves; through your guidance, support, and cultivation, they have ascended.
The common people dwell in a land of blessings; the Buddha-dharma relies upon a flourishing and prosperous age;
and the Buddhist monasteries were grandly established during the founding of the dynasty.

This humble and mediocre monk, [your] servant, is devoid of talent and too decrepit to endure further hardship. My abilities are no more than a small stream, yet I have been falsely honored to continue [the lineage].
The lamp’s delusion; my consciousness has strayed from the luminous teaching.

I am ashamed to have received such profound favor and bounty. Previously, I presented the complete collection of one hundred and twenty volumes, which early on opened the true eye of over seven thousand monks.
I reverently receive [your instructions].
The imperial decree has been respectfully entrusted to the craftsmen for carving. Having already been completed and adorned, it is hereby presented once more.
On this account, we again venture to make our request. We previously received the Emperor’s magnificent composition, which you had graciously promised [to bestow].
I venture to request that it be included in the Dragon Canon (Lóngzàng).
Having presumed to offend Your Majesty’s august presence, I humbly pray that—
The sagely virtue is lofty and towering, eternally establishing a foundation for ten thousand years.

The celestial river is vast and expansive, all of which ultimately returns to a single source. Rituals are perfected in the present age; the jade scrolls are matched with the nobility of brocade cases.
These matters surpass all antiquity; the golden wheel is firmly established upon the embroidered pillars in its majesty.
The auspicious reign shall be equal to the seven celestial bodies,
and the profound grace shall be as enduring as the two luminaries. How can I, the subject Sengchao, bear to gaze upon heaven and look up [in gratitude]?
Your Holiness, with the utmost urgency and trepidation, I respectfully submit this memorial for Your Majesty’s perusal.
I humbly present it.
Recorded on the [blank] day of the sixth month in the thirty-sixth year of the Kangxi era by the monk (Chao Yong).
General Preface to the Five Lamps Complete Record.

The *Dengshi zizhuan lianpu xuguang* (The Comprehensive Continuation and Expansion of the Lamp History Self-Biographies) in five volumes is a record of the Chan school that has long circulated in the world.
Subsequently, the Song dynasty Chan Master Dachuang Ji, deeming its scrolls too voluminous and its facts unverified,
deleted the spurious, corrected the erroneous, resolved doubts, and transmitted the authentic, binding them into [a single volume].
The *Huìyuán* (Compendium of the Source) is a work that possesses both scripture and dharma, as well as systematic order and underlying principle.

Regarding the lineage of the Chan tradition and its legal succession, it is clear, manifest, and evident without the need for further investigation. Its contribution to the Great Way and its benefit to students are immense;
it is truly a great classic within heaven and earth. Therefore, it is especially not something that can be equaled by other books.
This is a provisional assessment. Since these five hundred years, periods of clarity and obscurity have alternated; of the lineages of the Five Houses, only three remain.
Although the traditions of Linji and Caodong still persist, they no longer reflect the ancestral style of former times.

Moreover, in recent days, genealogical records have been repeatedly altered, and what we hear and see has become increasingly divergent—like the rushing of rivers and streams, where can one find a point of rest? As for the direct descendants...

"Whoever possesses blood and breath—how could they not look upon this with distress and feel profound sorrow? (Yong) I am ashamed before the former sages for my practice and feel abashed before the philosophers of old for my understanding.
Yet, mindful only of the sovereign's grace from above, I feel that even if I were to shatter my body, I could never repay it.
Thus, in the final years of my life, I have dragged my feet for thousands of li to seek out my fellow scholars and deliberate upon this book, so that we may together plan its completion."

Returning to antiquity, one suspends the salvation of those yet to come. Be upright and be cautious; be ultimate and be meticulous. I venture to say that this establishes a defense for all under heaven and for ten thousand generations.

Following the illustrious ways of the successive sagely emperors and compiling the essential methods of various schools, I have examined the past and verified the present, casting a net across both high and low.

Exhausting the mysteries of the spirit and pushing the limits of deliberation, I have depleted my wisdom and exhausted my abilities. The Dharma follows the rigorous regulations of the Spring and Autumn Annals and adheres to the urgent principles of the *Huìyuán*.

It also significantly clarifies the obscure and elucidates the subtle, revealing meanings not previously articulated by predecessors. May it be that through this, the principles shall flourish and the righteousness be fulfilled;
there must surely be those of enlightened wisdom who understand the music [of the truth], joining together to support the legacy of Sima Qian and Ban Gu. As for the sequence of its chapters:
Nanyue and Qingyuan both reached the thirty-seventh generation;
Tianwang [Yun] under Mazu and Tiantai (Tianhuang) under Shitou— these were all cases established by previous masters,
as seen in dozens of various canonical texts, all of which follow the *Lóngzàng Fózǔ Tōngzǎi* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the Central Plains).
This is based on the fundamental source, so that the lineage may remain without error.
The Compassionate Patriarch Haewon was Yong, not Po; he was two, not one. Alas, such is the result of their deluded and mistaken views.

To disparage my two lineages is surely not to know that "Universal Bestowal of Compassion" (Cija) refers to those mentioned in the inscription for Wanfeng Lenguang, while "Eternal Bestowal of Compassion" (Ciyong) corresponds to what is recorded in the monument for Dongming Yishan.
The principle is as clear as the light; what further need is there for debate?
The lineages of the Caodong school are recorded in various ways. I have now established this account by consulting Yongjue Xian’s *Supplement to the Lamp Record*,
Yuanmen Zhu’s *Continuation of the Abridged Record*, Han’u Kwan’s *Sequel to the Continuation*, and Weilin Pae’s *Dispelling Errors*,
synthesizing these sources to reach a definitive conclusion without resorting to personal bias.
Our own school is divided into five branches, primarily because it inherited the true lamp of China;
yet, without having personally attained realization within the same hall, one is not permitted to claim the status of a direct descendant who has transmitted the robe.

For instance, the ancient Jianfu [Monastery] happened upon the recorded words of the ancients on paper and, though more than a hundred years had passed since the time of the patriarch Yunmen Wenyan, it claimed to be his dharma heir.
To prioritize oneself excessively while treating the Dharma as insignificant is to disrupt the source of the Way and incur offense for a thousand ages.
Therefore, I venture to list these [lineages] under "Uncertain," in order to clarify that the transmission of the Dharma must never be confused and that one cannot hope for or rely upon empty claims.
Regarding the Elder Xueqiao Xin, it has long been said that no collected writings (cungao) of his transmission exist. Suddenly, Huang Duanduo, the Judicial Commissioner, appeared;
if Duanduo belongs to the Dongzong lineage, he might be included under Wuming Huijing or listed under Wuyi Yuanlai, as there is no fixed standard.
Upon carefully examining Duanduo’s detailed account of the origins of his succession, it is clear that he ultimately succeeded [to the lineage].
The *Xingzhuang* (Biographical Account) of Master Miyun Shouchang was composed by the Venerable Yanshou Wenyin. Aside from the twelve dharma heirs, there are no further branches or extensions.
Recently, Huang Yupiqi was added to the *Cangao* (Draft Collection), and Baoji was included among the disciples of Gusue.

O Wise One, I have not yet discerned the underlying intent or the life circumstances [of these figures]. Regarding the works composed by the patriarchs and sons of the Ratnakūṭa lineage, why are they not identical in this manner?
Since these two masters could not bear to let [their teachings] be lost, they modeled themselves after Yuan, Bai, Ke, Yi, Run, Shanchuang, Hai, and others;
yet they remain listed among those of "unknown details."
The layman Sengmo Ma Yiteng traveled extensively to seek instruction from masters throughout all quarters;
his realization was profound and accurate, and he proclaimed the Way among the regions of Wu, Yue, Yan, and Chu.

Among the scholar-officials, Taishi Lin Zengzhi, Si-nong Zhang Youyu, and Ji-xian Xiong Kaiyuan were all forged in his furnace. His writings on the unification of Confucianism and Chan—*Ruchan heyi*—...
The calligraphy is life-sized, a rarity even among the scholarly elite. [Details regarding] its inclusion remain unclear.
As for the holy sages who manifested through transformation: those from the Western Heaven (India) are listed at the end of the twenty-eight patriarchs, while those from the Eastern Land (China)...
They were gathered before Nan Yue and Qing Yuan so that the sequence might be clearly discerned and the order of principles not confused.
As for the records of ancient and modern venerable masters that still exist, their words have been selected separately; we do not follow the old texts. If there are none...

This record may be compiled by following various texts from the *Dengyuan* (Lamp Source) tradition, extracting the essentials and deleting the redundancies; what is valued is the accuracy and appropriateness of the underlying intent.
The names of the lineages of the five schools shall all follow those recorded in various genealogical charts (*pǔ*), provided they are supported by biographies and Dharma discourses.
As for those whose names were taken from preceding sources but whose chapter order was not established, their catalogs are placed at the end.

From the thirty-fifth, thirty-sixth, and thirty-seventh generations below Nanyue, and the thirty-seventh generation below Qingyuan, the branches have proliferated so extensively that it is difficult to obtain them in their entirety;
therefore, these are recorded as they are obtained, following only the sequence of the generations.
Without regard for the chronological order of the succession of the Dharma,
this was written by the śramaṇa Chaoyong, a successor from Shuzili, on the first day of the Upper Month in the Jiazi year of the Kangxi era, at the Shenxue Caotang (Deep Snow Hermitage).

The Seven Buddhas—
Vipaśyin Buddha and Śikhin Buddha.
Vipaśyin Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha,
Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha,
and Śākyamuni Buddha.
The Patriarch Mahākāśyapa of the Western Heaven; the Venerable Ānanda;
the Venerable Śaṇavāsa; and the Venerable Upagupta.
Venerable Dīdaka; Venerable Miñjaka;
Venerable Vasumitra; Venerable Buddhanandi;
